title: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections)
hook: one Upanishad sentence says what the self is not, and then what it is, and Ramanuja builds on holding both halves

segments.voice: Yesterday opened Vaishnava theology with Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, the book that states the other view first.
screen: `THE OTHER VIEW FIRST.` · `TODAY: WITHOUT, AND WITH.`

segments.voice: Free from evil. Free from old age. Free from death, from grief, from hunger, from thirst. That's how the Chandogya Upanishad begins describing the self worth seeking. A long run of withouts. And then, in the same breath, the sentence turns. Whose desires are real. Whose resolves come true. Suddenly there's someone there: someone who wants, and whose wanting is never empty. One sentence, two halves, a no and a yes. Some readers lean on the first half. Ramanuja says you have to keep both.
screen: `FREE FROM EVIL, AGE, DEATH, GRIEF.` → `THEN: WHOSE DESIRES ARE REAL.` → `A NO AND A YES.`

segments.voice: The Upanishads sometimes call Brahman nirguna, without qualities. Other passages pile qualities on: all-knowing, all-powerful, the source of joy. How do you read a text that seems to say both? Advaita teachers, in Shankara's line, read the withouts as the highest truth, and the qualities as true from where people stand, a lower vantage. Ramanuja, in the Sri Bhashya, reads it another way. Without qualities, he says, means without bad qualities: no evil, no decay, no limit, no lack. And the qualities the texts praise, knowledge, power, compassion, beauty, are fully real in Brahman. So the no and the yes aren't two levels. They're one portrait drawn from both sides: everything wrong ruled out, everything good affirmed. Sri Vaishnava teachers call Brahman an ocean of auspicious qualities. That's why the Chandogya sentence matters so much to him: it shows the pattern inside a single line, and neither half cancels the other. For Ramanuja, this has a human side. A God with every good quality and no flaw is someone you can bring a grief to, or sing to, as the Alvars did. His theology and their devotion meet right here. Both schools argue carefully from the same Upanishads, and both have their reasons; this is a chance to hear Ramanuja clearly, not to rank them.
screen: `NIRGUNA: WITHOUT QUALITIES.` · `WITHOUT BAD QUALITIES.` · `AN OCEAN OF GOOD QUALITIES.` · `SOMEONE YOU CAN TALK TO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love. First the withouts: for a few breaths, set down every complaint you have about them, what they forgot, what annoys you. Then the yes: name quietly the good that's really in them, their patience, their laugh, the way they show up; if you pray, turn the same no and yes toward the name you pray to.
Vaishnava theology. Today, without qualities read as without bad qualities, and an ocean of good ones: a no and a yes in one portrait.
Your line: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections). Every fault ruled out, every good thing affirmed. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas study the Sri Bhashya's reading of nirguna with a teacher, and in worship they praise Vishnu and Lakshmi through their qualities, in hymns, names and stotras that list the Lord's good qualities one by one.

fork.setup: you're Ramanuja. one Upanishad says Brahman is without qualities, another praises Brahman's knowledge and power. how do you read them together?
options: without qualities means without bad qualities; the good ones are real.
only the qualities are real; ignore the withouts.
the texts contradict each other; pick one.
fork.reveal: Ramanuja reads the no and the yes as one portrait: every fault ruled out, every good quality affirmed.

original.note: Sanskrit: without qualities. Ramanuja reads it as without bad qualities.

trapdoor: what you thought: nirguna means God has no qualities.
what it means: for Ramanuja, it means no bad qualities, while every good quality is real.
what a scholar hears: the Chandogya 8.1.5 and 8.7.1 pattern, apahatapapma and satyakama, read as Brahman's two marks: free of all faults, full of auspicious qualities.

chat.says: If Brahman is 'without qualities', how can Ramanuja call God loving and wise?
options: For him, without qualities means without bad ones; the good ones are fully real.
He skips the without-qualities passages, since they don't fit his view.
He says Brahman gains good qualities only after the world is made.
chat.meaning: Ramanuja reads nirguna as free of every fault, while knowledge, power, compassion and beauty are fully real in Brahman.

nirguna.meaning: without qualities; for Ramanuja, without bad qualities

Advaita.meaning: non-dual Vedanta, the school of Shankara's line

Shankara.meaning: the great teacher of Advaita Vedanta

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.7.1 (the self free from evil, age, death, grief, hunger and thirst, whose desires and resolves are real)
Ramanuja, Sri Bhashya, on nirguna and saguna texts (e.g. under 1.1.1 and 3.2)

notes: Chandogya 8.7.1 (and 8.1.5) is paraphrased; Max Müller's 1879 SBE translation exists but the exact wording wasn't certain, so nothing is quoted.
Advaita's reading is summarized in one sentence (the qualities true from a lower vantage, vyavaharika); an Advaita reader should confirm it is fair.
Where exactly in the Sri Bhashya Ramanuja makes the 'without bad qualities' argument most clearly should be checked; references given loosely.
'Ocean of auspicious qualities' (kalyana-guna-akara) is a standard Sri Vaishnava phrase; confirm wording.
